chunks: My father narrated (may God be pleased with him) said: Sa'd ibn Abdullah narrated, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa, from his father, from Hammad ibn Isa, from Umar ibn Azineh, from Aban ibn Abi Ayyash, from Sulaym ibn Qays al-Hilali, who said: I heard the Commander of the Faithful, Ali (peace be upon him), say:

Beware regarding your religion of three: A man who recited the Quran until, when you saw the brightness of it upon his face, he drew his sword against his neighbor and accused him of polytheism. I said: 'O Commander of the Faithful, which one is more deserving of polytheism?' He said: 'The accuser.' And a man who was captivated by hadiths; whenever you told him a lie, he extended it to be longer than it was. And a man to whom God Almighty granted authority, who claimed that his obedience is God's obedience and his disobedience is God's disobedience — and he lied, because there is no obedience to a creature in the disobedience of the Creator. It is not fitting for a creature to love disobedience to God, so there is no obedience in his disobedience, nor obedience to one who disobeys God. Indeed, obedience is for God, His Messenger, and the Trustees of Affairs. And God Almighty commanded obedience to the Messenger because he is infallible and pure, who does not command disobedience to Him. And He commanded obedience to the Trustees of Affairs because they are infallible and pure, who do not command disobedience to Him.

key_terms.الرَّامِي: The accuser (one who makes the accusation of kufr)
key_terms.الْحَادِيثُ: Hadiths (narrations/stories, here referring to oral traditions or tales)
key_terms.بَهْجَتُهُ: The brightness or radiance of the Quran on the face

ai.seo_question: What are the three people to beware of in one's religion according to Imam Ali?
ai.summary: This narration from al-Khisal highlights the phenomenon of 'Tajassus' (excessive scrutiny) in early Islamic history, where Quran recitors like Muawiyah's forces killed companions for perceived minor deviations, illustrating that the accuser often bears greater guilt than the accused. It further critiques the 'Taqleed al-Sultan' (imitation of the ruler) where leaders claim divine authority, contrasting this with the Shia doctrine of 'Ma'sumiyyah' (infallibility) which ensures that obedience to the Prophet and the Imams is strictly tied to their divine guidance without error. The hadith establishes the hierarchy of obedience, linking the Prophet's authority to his purity and the Imams' authority to their status as Infallible Trustees, thereby grounding political legitimacy in spiritual infallibility.
